extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in scientometrics, research evaluation, and peer review studies (interested in gender bias in grant review)
extracted.subtask_short: gender bias in grant peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Reanalyzing and measuring gender bias in grant-panel peer review: methods for measuring performance, reviewer scoring, nepotism effects, and whether panel score bias translates into funding decisions. Focus is on replication / reanalysis of Wennerås & Wold using field- and panel-level adjustments and statistical modelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-normalizing the performance scores
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust applicants' performance indicators to account for differences between scientific fields (the paper states: 'After field-normalizing the performance scores...'). This is used to make publication/productivity metrics comparable across fields and was applied here as in the original W&W data to avoid confounding by disciplinary variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel-standardizing the review scores
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize review scores within panels to account for panel-specific scoring scales or tendencies ('panel-standardizing the review scores'). This addresses between-panel differences in stringency or mean scores so comparisons across panels are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of the 'male bonus' in terms of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The well-known 1997 study found a ‘male bonus’ of three Science papers: women would need three additional publications in Science to get a similar score for their competence as men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize gender advantage/disadvantage as the additional measurable output (e.g., number of high-profile papers) women would need to reach equivalent competence scores. Use comparable bibliometric indicators (e.g., Science/Nature papers) to quantify the 'male bonus'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess gender bias in competence scores
rubrics_metrics.description: We did find gender bias in the competence scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly test whether competence/merit scores assigned by reviewers differ by applicant gender after controlling for performance and other covariates. Report effect sizes (e.g., male bonus) and their sensitivity to modelling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer affiliation (nepotism) bonus
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether applicants with reviewer-affiliated institutions or known connections receive systematically higher scores. Control for affiliation and proximity in models to separate nepotism effects from merit signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation letter bonus
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the presence/strength/content of recommendation letters correlates with higher review scores or success, and whether this interacts with applicant gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate whether panel-score bias leads to bias in grant decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: We have expanded the original study by investigating whether there is any bias in the grant decisions, an issue not discussed by Wennerås and Wold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stop at reviewer scores — model the link from panel scores to final funding decisions (binary outcome). Assess whether observed bias in scores translates into differential funding rates by gender, and test this at both aggregate and panel levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel-level analysis (disaggregate by panel)
rubrics_metrics.description: research into gender bias in grant allocation should be conducted at the panel level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform analyses separately or include interactions for each evaluation panel because bias may vary by panel. The paper notes that two panels accounted for a substantial share of female applicants and showed bias in grant decisions; aggregated analysis can mask panel-specific effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use same performance measures as original study for replication
rubrics_metrics.description: As this is a reanalysis, we include performance in the analysis in the same way as W&W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For faithful replication, use the original operationalization of performance indicators. When deviating, document and justify changes, and test robustness to the original measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods: GLMs and regressions; obtain (pseudo) R2
rubrics_metrics.description: SPSS27, generalized linear models (linear model and logistic model). As GLMs does not provide R2, the analyses were also done with linear and logistic regression to obtain the values for the (pseudo) R2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate statistical models (linear models for continuous outcomes, logistic for binary funding outcomes). If using GLMs that do not report R2, run complementary regression analyses to obtain R2 / pseudo-R2 for model comparison and explanatory power reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include age / year of birth as covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Age was also found to be associated with grant success and career success in other studies... W&W did not use year of birth, but in another study on early career postdocs we found a significant effect of age: younger is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for applicant age (or year of birth) because it can be associated with both productivity and funding success and may confound gender effects. Report whether inclusion changes gender-bias estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks on sample composition
rubrics_metrics.description: We did the analysis also with the 116 applicants, and that did not change the findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform sensitivity analyses using different sample selections (e.g., reduced sample sizes, subsets) to check stability of results. Report whether conclusions hold under alternative samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize success rates relative to broader population or council
rubrics_metrics.description: Table shows that the overall success rate for men at the SMC was about 50%, and the female success rate would be between 40 and 45... In the grant scheme under study, the male and female success rates are 26% and 8% respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed success rates in the study sample to wider institutional or scheme-level rates to assess whether the sampled year/scheme is typical or exceptional. Use this to interpret observed gaps and avoid overgeneralizing from exceptional snapshots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document dataset provenance and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: After this paper was accepted, we were notified that Ulf Sandström and Ulla Riis recently published ... after implementing corrections in the deployed dataset... They arrive at different conclusions than we do because we use the original data we received from Sandström and also deployed a different analytical approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly document data sources, any corrections or dataset versions used, and how analytic choices differ from other reanalyses. Acknowledge that dataset corrections or different analytical approaches can change conclusions; where possible make data and code available or cite supplementary materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that normalization/standardization choices affect measured bias magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: After field-normalizing the performance scores and panel-standardizing the review scores, we found partly different results... the male bonus we found is only one-fifth of the male bonus reported by Wennerås and Wold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent that methodological choices (e.g., field normalization, panel standardization) materially affect effect sizes for gender bias. Present alternative specifications and explain how each adjustment influences estimated bias.
